title: The Law of Sines and the Law of Cosines

TE5-F-01.hint: When two angles are known, the third is \(180\text{°}\) minus their sum. With an angle and its opposite side known, use \(\dfrac{\sin A}{a} = \dfrac{\sin B}{b}\) to find another side.
slips: Using the Law of Sines without a matching angle and opposite side.
Forgetting to find the third angle first.
Pairing a side with an angle that is not opposite it.

TE5-F-02.hint: With three sides and no angle, use the Law of Cosines: \(\cos A = \dfrac{b^{2} + c^{2} - a^{2}}{2bc}\). The side whose square is subtracted is the one opposite the angle.
slips: Subtracting the wrong side's square. The side opposite the angle is the one subtracted.
Stopping at the cosine and not applying the inverse cosine.

TE5-F-03.hint: Two sides and the angle between them: use the Law of Cosines for the third side, \(c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\cos C\), and take a square root. Then find another angle and subtract from \(180\text{°}\) for the last one.
slips: Subtracting before multiplying, such as \((a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab)\cos C\).
Using the Law of Sines first, when there is no angle with its opposite side.
Reporting \(c^{2}\) as \(c\), without taking the square root.

TE5-A-01.hint: Two sides and an angle opposite one of them can give no triangle, one triangle, or two. Use the Law of Sines to find \(\sin B\). If it is greater than \(1\) there is no triangle. Otherwise \(B\) and \(180\text{°} - B\) are both candidates, and each stays only if the three angles can still add to \(180\text{°}\).
slips: Stopping after the first angle and missing the second triangle.
Keeping \(180\text{°} - B\) when \(A + (180\text{°} - B)\) is already \(180\text{°}\) or more.
Saying there is no solution because the sine is less than \(1\).

parts.q: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 74\text{°}\), \(B = 55\text{°}\), and \(a = 23\). Find \(C\), \(b\), and \(c\) (round sides to the nearest tenth). State which law you used and why.
parts.a: Two angles are known, so \(C = 180\text{°} - 74\text{°} - 55\text{°} = 51\text{°}\). We know an angle and the side opposite it (\(A\) and \(a\)), so use the Law of Sines: \(b = \dfrac{23\sin 55\text{°}}{\sin 74\text{°}} \approx 19.6\) and \(c = \dfrac{23\sin 51\text{°}}{\sin 74\text{°}} \approx 18.6\).

parts.q: In triangle \(ABC\), \(a = 8\), \(b = 11\), and \(c = 14\). Find all three angles (round to the nearest tenth of a degree). State which law you used and why.

In the same way, \(B \approx 51.6\text{°}\) and \(C \approx 93.6\text{°}\). Check: the angles add to \(180\text{°}\).

parts.q: In triangle \(ABC\), \(A = 42\text{°}\), \(a = 8\), and \(b = 11\). Determine whether zero, one, or two triangles exist, and solve for all valid triangles (round angles to the nearest tenth of a degree and sides to the nearest tenth).
parts.a: Use the Law of Sines: \(\sin B = \dfrac{11\sin 42\text{°}}{8} \approx 0.9201\). Since \(11\sin 42\text{°} \lt  8 \lt  11\), there are two triangles. Triangle 1: \(B \approx 66.9\text{°}\), \(C \approx 71.1\text{°}\), \(c \approx 11.3\). Triangle 2: \(B \approx 180\text{°} - 66.9\text{°} = 113.1\text{°}\), \(C \approx 24.9\text{°}\), \(c \approx 5.0\).

parts.a: Use the Law of Sines: \(\sin B = \dfrac{20\sin 38\text{°}}{25} \approx 0.4925\), so \(B \approx 29.5\text{°}\). The other angle with this sine, \(180\text{°} - B\), is too large because side \(a\) is longer than side \(b\) (so \(A\) is larger than \(B\)). There is one triangle: \(C \approx 112.5\text{°}\) and \(c \approx 37.5\).

Triangle 1: \(B \approx 49.7\text{°}\), \(C \approx 97.3\text{°}\), \(c \approx 18.2\). Triangle 2: \(B \approx 180\text{°} - 49.7\text{°} = 130.3\text{°}\), \(C \approx 16.7\text{°}\), \(c \approx 5.3\).
